title: Question 2
stem:
A ball on horizontal ground is kicked towards a vertical wall. Fig. 2.1 shows the path of the ball.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

Fig. 2.1 (not to scale)

The ball has an initial velocity $u$ at an angle of $38^\circ$ to the ground. The ball travels a horizontal distance of $9.0\text{ m}$ before striking the wall at a height $h$ above the ground. The horizontal component $u_{H}$ of the initial velocity of the ball is $9.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Air resistance is negligible.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Show that the time $t$ for the ball to reach the wall is $0.95\text{ s}$.
hints: Hint 1: Think separately about the horizontal journey to the wall. With air resistance negligible, what happens to the horizontal component of velocity during the flight?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate Horizontal From Vertical**
You are sitting beside me looking at a projectile. My golden rule is to always split it into two independent motions. Horizontally there is no force (no air resistance), so the horizontal velocity stays constant at $u_H = 9.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ all the way to the wall.

Step 2: **Use Constant Speed To Find Time**
For constant velocity, distance = speed x time. So for the $9.0\text{ m}$ horizontal distance:
$$t = \frac{\text{horizontal distance}}{u_H} = \frac{9.0}{9.5} = 0.947\text{ s} \approx 0.95\text{ s}$$

enrichment.label: (a)(i)
key_concepts: projectile motion independence of horizontal and vertical motion
uniform horizontal velocity with no air resistance
hints: Hint 1: Think separately about the horizontal journey to the wall. With air resistance negligible, what happens to the horizontal component of velocity during the flight?

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the vertical component $u_{V}$ of the initial velocity of the ball.

markscheme_points.text: (uV) = 9.5 tan 38° or 9.5 / tan 52° or 9.5 = u cos 38° and uV = u sin 38° or 9.5 = u cos 38° and uV = (u² - 9.5²)½

hints: Hint 1: Sketch the initial velocity $u$ at $38^{\circ}$ to the horizontal as an arrow. Which side of the right-angled triangle is $u_H$ and which side is $u_V$?
Hint 2: Relate the opposite and adjacent sides of that $38^{\circ}$ triangle using $\tan 38^{\circ} = u_V / u_H$, then rearrange for $u_V$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture The Velocity Triangle**
Imagine $u$ as the hypotenuse at $38^{\circ}$ above the ground. The base is the horizontal component $u_H = 9.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the vertical side is $u_V$ that you need. Opposite over adjacent links them.

Step 2: **Calculate The Vertical Component**
From trigonometry:
$$\tan 38^{\circ} = \frac{u_V}{u_H}$$
$$u_V = u_H \tan 38^{\circ} = 9.5 \times \tan 38^{\circ}$$
$$u_V = 7.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (a)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Now focus only on vertical motion. The ball starts upward with the $u_V$ you just found, but gravity pulls down the whole time. List $u$, $a$, $t$ for the vertical direction with a clear sign convention.
Hint 2: Choose the displacement equation that links $s$, $u$, $a$ and $t$ with no final velocity needed, then substitute $u_V$, $a = -9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $t = 0.95\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set Up Vertical Motion**
Take upwards as positive. Then initial vertical velocity $u = u_V = 7.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$, acceleration $a = -g = -9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$, time $t = 0.95\text{ s}$, and displacement $s = h$. Gravity slows the upward rise, so the $\frac{1}{2}at^2$ term will subtract.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The speed of the ball just after striking the wall is less than its speed just before striking the wall.

State what this indicates about the nature of the collision of the ball with the wall.
hints: Hint 1: If speed drops, what happens to $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$? Recall the test that distinguishes an elastic collision from an inelastic one.
parts.proper_answer: The collision is inelastic as kinetic energy is not conserved.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Speed To Kinetic Energy**
Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. A smaller speed after hitting the wall means less kinetic energy after than before, even though momentum behaviour may be different.

Step 2: **Name The Collision Type**
An elastic collision keeps total kinetic energy the same. Here energy is lost, for example as sound and heat and deformation of the ball and wall. So this indicates an inelastic collision.
